content: Lipid emulsions (LEs) are an essential component of parenteral nutrition (PN) for critically ill term and late preterm infants, particularly those with gastrointestinal failure. Traditional soybean oil-based lipid emulsions (S-LEs) contain high levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and phytosterols, which may contribute to complications such as parenteral nutrition-associated liver disease (PNALD). The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of various LEs used in PN for term and late preterm infants (34 to 36 weeks and 6 days of gestation) with or without surgical conditions or PNALD during the first six months of life. The review included all possible direct comparisons of LEs. The search strategy involved multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, as well as trial registries and conference proceedings. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials were included. Data collection and analysis followed Cochrane Neonatal methods, and the GRADE approach was used to assess the quality of evidence. Nine randomized studies involving 273 infants were included. LEs were categorized into three groups: (1) fish oil-containing LEs (e.g., pure fish oil [F-LE] and multisource LEs such as medium-chain triglycerides [MCT]-olive-fish-soybean oil [MOFS-LE], MCT-fish-soy oil [MFS-LE], and olive-fish-soy [OFS-LE]); (2) conventional pure S-LEs; and (3) alternative LEs (e.g., MCT-soy [MS-LE], olive-soy [OS-LE], and borage oil-based LEs). Four comparisons were analyzed: (1) fish oil-containing LEs versus non-fish oil LEs, (2) fish oil-containing LEs versus other fish oil-containing LEs, (3) alternative LEs versus S-LEs, and (4) alternative LEs versus other alternative LEs. In infants with surgical conditions and no pre-existing PNALD, meta-analysis showed no significant difference in the incidence of PNALD/cholestasis (defined as conjugated bilirubin [Cbil] ≥ 2 mg/dL) between fish oil-containing LEs and S-LEs (risk ratio [RR] 1.20, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.38 to 3.76; risk difference [RD] 0.03, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.20; 2 studies, n = 68; low-quality evidence). In infants with PNALD/cholestasis, fish oil-containing LEs were associated with significantly lower rates of cholestasis compared to S-LEs (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.91; RD -0.39, 95% CI -0.65 to -0.12; number needed to treat for benefit [NNTB] 3, 95% CI 2 to 9; 2 studies, n = 40; very low-quality evidence). However, the small sample size and methodological differences between studies increased uncertainty about these findings. One study in infants with cholestasis reported significantly better weight gain with pure fish oil LEs compared to 10% S-LEs (45 g/week, 95% CI 15.0 to 75.0; n = 16; very low-quality evidence). No significant differences in growth parameters were observed in studies involving surgical populations. For secondary outcomes, one study (n = 24) in infants with cholestasis reported significantly lower conjugated bilirubin levels but higher gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) levels with MOFS-LE (SMOFlipid) compared to S-LE (Intralipid). Another study (n = 16), which was terminated early, reported significantly higher alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and conjugated bilirubin levels in the S-LE group compared to pure F-LE (Omegaven). In surgical infants, two studies each reported on hypertriglyceridemia and conjugated bilirubin levels, with conflicting results between studies. Meta-analysis was not performed due to high heterogeneity and limited data. There was no evidence of differences in mortality, sepsis, alkaline phosphatase, or ALT levels in infants with surgical conditions or cholestasis (very low-quality evidence). Neurodevelopmental outcomes at six and 24 months were reported in one study (n = 11) involving surgical infants, with no significant differences between pure F-LE and S-LE groups. Another study in infants with cholestasis (n = 16) found no difference in head growth velocity between pure F-LE and S-LE groups. The quality of evidence ranged from low to very low due to the small sample sizes, single-center designs, and early termination of three of the six studies contributing data to the review. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence from randomized studies to determine the potential benefits of fish oil-containing LEs or other LEs over S-LEs for the prevention or resolution of PNALD/cholestasis or other outcomes in term and late preterm infants with surgical conditions or cholestasis. No studies were identified in infants without surgical conditions or cholestasis. Further research is needed to clarify the role of fish oil and other lipid sources in improving clinical outcomes in parenterally fed term and late preterm infants.
